solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Dined out, having photo taken?

blocks.note: pic is short for picture, a photo
nicked is British slang for stolen, taken

explanation.surface: Someone eats at a restaurant and has their photo snapped, perhaps by paparazzi.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Having photo taken' reads as one idea, but it splits into two pieces: a photo, then a word meaning taken. 'Nicked' is everyday British slang for stolen.
explanation.definitionFit: To picnic is to eat a meal outdoors, so dining out in the open air fits the past tense.

clue.text: Optimistic, I have to go out, advance

indicators.note: what goes out leaves the room, so these letters must leave the word they sit in

blocks.note: positive means hopeful, optimistic
the contraction I've, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A hopeful speaker decides to leave and move forward.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like three separate commands; really 'I have' is written as I'VE and removed from the end of POSITIVE, leaving POSIT.
explanation.definitionFit: To posit a theory is to put it forward for consideration, which is what advancing an idea means.

clue.text: I control a fan, not somehow wanting to encourage hostility

indicators.note: somehow means in some unspecified way, so the letters are arranged in some way not yet given

blocks.note: the letters taken as written, all fifteen of them

explanation.surface: Someone boasts of controlling a supporter, oddly not wanting to stir up trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface seems to deny hostility with 'not', but 'not' is just three more letters in the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: A confrontational person seeks out conflict and argument, provoking the aggression and enmity the clue describes.

clue.text: Unusual language with which the French attempt to convey adulation

blocks.note: Ido is a little-used constructed language, an offshoot of Esperanto
la is French for 'the' (feminine)
a try is an attempt

explanation.surface: Someone tries to express adoration in an odd tongue, with French thrown in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unusual' looks like an anagram signal, but here it just describes the language: Ido, an obscure invented one.
explanation.definitionFit: Idolatry is excessive worship or admiration of a person, a stronger form of fawning praise.

clue.text: Monarch bags a hairy beast in sport

indicators.note: to bag something is to put it in a bag, so one piece is placed inside another

blocks.note: a king is a monarch
taken as written
the yak is a long-haired Himalayan ox

explanation.surface: A king goes hunting and shoots, or bags, a shaggy animal for sport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bags' suggests a hunter's haul, which fits the sporting surface, but it only signals that the monarch wraps around the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Kayaking, paddling a small covered canoe, is a water sport and recreational activity.

clue.text: Explain sea fish being found in fresh water

indicators.note: something found in a place sits inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: the Dee is a river, a body of fresh water
the cod is a sea fish

explanation.surface: A puzzled observer asks why a saltwater fish turns up in a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fresh water' is a river, the Dee, which runs between England and Wales and also through Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: To decode a message is to work out and make plain its meaning, so interpreting or clarifying it.

clue.text: US agent without hesitation vented anger

indicators.note: in its old sense without means outside, so one piece stands around another

blocks.note: a fed is an American federal agent, an FBI man
um is the sound of hesitation

explanation.surface: An American agent loses his temper without pausing for a moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' seems to mean lacking, but it is read as outside: the agent goes around the hesitation.
explanation.definitionFit: To fume is to seethe or rage, so the past tense describes someone who expressed fury.

clue.text: Great guy who belongs to a left-wing society

definitions.text: who belongs to a left-wing society
definitions.note: a relative clause standing for a noun: one who belongs

blocks.note: fab, short for fabulous, means great
Ian is a man's name, any guy

explanation.surface: A splendid fellow happens to be a member of a socialist club.
explanation.walkthrough: The Fabian Society is a British socialist think tank linked to the Labour Party; a Fabian is a member.
explanation.definitionFit: A Fabian is a member of the Fabian Society, a gradualist socialist organisation founded in 1884.

clue.text: Stolen data — I promise, when grilled, to keep very quiet, right?

indicators.note: grilled food is cooked and changed, so these letters are reworked into a new order
to keep something is to hold it, so one set of letters holds another inside

blocks.note: the letters taken as written
pp, pianissimo, is the musical mark for very quiet
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A suspect questioned about stolen data promises, under interrogation, to stay silent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grilled' fits the interrogation picture, but it signals the anagram; the musical mark for very quiet and the right go inside the rearranged letters, not into the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: To misappropriate is to take dishonestly for one's own use, so embezzled or purloined goods have been misappropriated.

clue.text: Resistance in party with nothing to lose to change? Shame!

indicators.note: what is lost is no longer there, so a letter is dropped
a thing in something else is placed inside it
with means alongside, so pieces are set next to each other

blocks.note: a disco is a dance party
O looks like zero, nothing
R is the symbol for electrical resistance
to edit is to change

explanation.surface: Opposition within a political party that has nothing to lose from reform is scorned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' wants to be political, but it is a dance party; 'nothing to lose' means that party drops its O, and resistance goes in before the change.
explanation.definitionFit: To discredit someone is to harm their reputation, bringing disgrace or dishonour upon them.

clue.text: Yr nose’s constructed to be this?

definitions.text: Yr nose’s constructed to be this?

indicators.note: something constructed is built from parts, so the letters are assembled into a new form

blocks.note: the letters taken as written, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A question about why your nose was built: surely for smelling things?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yr' is an informal abbreviation of your, used here only for its letters. The whole clue is both wordplay and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The nose is an organ built for smelling, one of the five senses, so it is by design a sense organ.

clue.text: Painters given copper coins outside front of shop

indicators.note: the front of a word is its first letter
to be outside something is to surround it, so one piece goes around another
given means added to, so one piece is set beside another

blocks.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
bits are small coins, as in a threepenny bit
first letter of shop

explanation.surface: Artists are paid in small change, standing outside a shop front.
explanation.walkthrough: A bit is a British word for a small coin, as in the old threepenny bit. 'Copper' also suggests pennies, but here it is the metal.
explanation.definitionFit: Cubists, such as Picasso and Braque, were artists who broke subjects into geometric shapes.

clue.text: Devon swimmer cheers when rescue vessel comes in

indicators.note: whatever comes in enters, so it ends up inside another piece

blocks.note: ta is British informal thanks, cheers
Noah's ark rescued the animals from the flood

explanation.surface: A swimmer off the Devon coast cheers as a lifeboat arrives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheers' in Britain can mean thanks, like ta. The swimmer is no person: Tarka is the otter of Henry Williamson's novel, set on Devon's rivers.
explanation.definitionFit: Tarka the Otter lives in the rivers of north Devon, a famous fictional animal that swims.

clue.text: Child brought before head, one to get child removed?

indicators.note: what is brought before something is placed ahead of it, so pieces go in order

blocks.note: a kid is a child
napper is old British slang for the head

explanation.surface: A pupil is sent to the headteacher, who then arranges for the child to be expelled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' suggests a headteacher, but it is the body part, in the slang word napper.
explanation.definitionFit: A kidnapper abducts people, often children, taking them away by force for ransom.

clue.text: Getting to the heart of money people engaged in illegal activity?

blocks.note: a cent is a coin, some money
a ring is a criminal gang, as in a smuggling ring

explanation.surface: Investigators get to the bottom of a money-laundering operation.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests one phrase about finance crime; it splits into a coin and a gang.
explanation.definitionFit: Centring means moving to the middle point, so it is reaching the core of something.

clue.text: They are hard to name, having zero applications

indicators.note: having means possessing as well, so pieces are joined one after another

blocks.note: to call someone something is to name them
O looks like zero
uses are applications

explanation.surface: Useless things are difficult to put a name to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'They are hard to name' reads as one idea, but the definition stops at 'hard'.
explanation.definitionFit: Callouses are thickened, toughened patches of skin, so they are firm growths on hands or feet.

clue.text: Wadi may be this little river needing help to get across

indicators.note: to get across something is to span it, so one piece stretches around another

blocks.note: aid is help
R is the abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: Crossing a small river in a dry valley, you might need assistance.
explanation.walkthrough: A wadi is a desert valley, dry except in the rainy season.
explanation.definitionFit: A wadi is a watercourse in the desert that is usually without water, so it is parched.

clue.text: Influence of guy in bank

indicators.note: a thing in something else is placed inside it

blocks.note: a levee is a raised river bank
to guy someone is to mock them, as does to rag

explanation.surface: A man working in a bank has sway over things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guy' looks like a man and 'bank' a financial one; guy is a verb meaning tease, and bank is the side of a river.
explanation.definitionFit: Leverage is power to affect outcomes, the advantage or sway one party holds over another.

clue.text: Bad eggs showing certain characteristics, stealing gold

indicators.note: to steal something is to take it in, so one piece is held inside another

blocks.note: traits are characteristics
or is the heraldic word for gold

explanation.surface: Villains reveal their true nature by pilfering gold.
explanation.walkthrough: Or is gold in heraldry, a common crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: Bad eggs are rotten, untrustworthy people, and a turncoat who betrays his country is one kind.

clue.text: Learner, fool — what one isn’t using?

blocks.note: L is for learner, as on a British L-plate
an oaf is a clumsy fool

explanation.surface: A beginner is called an idiot and asked what they are failing to use.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Use your loaf' is British for 'think': loaf of bread is rhyming slang for head. A fool is someone not using theirs.
explanation.definitionFit: In rhyming slang, loaf of bread means head, and an idiot is plainly not using his brain.

clue.text: At end of month engineers coming to mine ruined by neglect

indicators.note: what comes at the end of something follows it, so one piece is placed after another
coming to means arriving next to, so pieces are joined in sequence

blocks.note: Dec is the abbreviation for December
RE is the Royal Engineers of the British Army
a pit is a coal mine

explanation.surface: Engineers arrive at a mine at the end of the month to find it derelict.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At end of month' looks like a date, but it places the engineers after the month.
explanation.definitionFit: Decrepit describes something worn out and dilapidated from age or lack of care.

clue.text: Curious type like Bond trapping his adversary with love

indicators.note: to trap something is to enclose it, so one piece goes around another
with means alongside, so pieces are set together

blocks.note: James Bond is a spy
Dr No is Bond's villain in the first film
love is zero in tennis, O

explanation.surface: An inquisitive person resembling James Bond captures his enemy and romance too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Curious type' reads as the definition, but 'type' belongs to the wordplay: 'type like Bond' is SPY.
explanation.definitionFit: Snoopy means nosy, prying into others' business, which is inquisitiveness in its unwelcome form.

clue.text: Rocker’s enemy, imprisoned individual, languished

indicators.note: something imprisoned is locked inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: Mods and Rockers were rival British youth gangs of the 1960s
one is a single individual

explanation.surface: A rock musician's foe, locked away, wasted away in a cell.
explanation.walkthrough: Mods, on scooters, and Rockers, on motorbikes, famously brawled at British seaside towns in the 1960s.
explanation.definitionFit: To moon about is to drift listlessly and pine, which is the idle, dreamy drooping of languishing.

clue.text: Feature of eastern churches making one in mood change

indicators.note: to change something is to alter it, so the letters take a different form

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Something about Orthodox churches puts a visitor in a different frame of mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mood change' reads as a noun phrase, but 'change' acts on the letters before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Onion-shaped domes crown many Russian and Eastern Orthodox churches, a signature architectural element.

clue.text: Climbers struggle with first sign of snow on island

indicators.note: the first sign of a word is its opening letter
in an across clue, one thing on another comes after it

blocks.note: I is the abbreviation for island
to vie is to struggle or compete
first letter of snow

explanation.surface: Mountaineers battle against the first snowfall on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Climbers' suggests mountaineers, but it means climbing plants.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivy is a creeping evergreen plant that grows up walls and trees, so ivies are climbing plants.

clue.text: Victorian child labourer? Little son to cry

blocks.note: s is the abbreviation for son
to weep is to cry

explanation.surface: A small boy sent to work in Victorian times is left in tears.
explanation.walkthrough: Victorian chimney sweeps sent small boys up inside chimneys; the question mark flags the definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Chimney sweeps in nineteenth-century Britain used young boys to climb and clean flues.

clue.text: Hospital not functioning in seaside town

blocks.note: a san is short for sanatorium, a hospital
a system that is down is not working

explanation.surface: A hospital in a coastal resort has broken down.
explanation.walkthrough: Sandown is a resort on the Isle of Wight, off England's south coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Sandown is a beach resort on the east coast of the Isle of Wight, a holiday destination.

clue.text: An extreme part of the world penetrated by saint and missionary

indicators.note: what is penetrated has something pushed into it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.clueFragment: An extreme part of the world
blocks.note: a pole is the northernmost or southernmost point of the globe
St is the abbreviation for saint

explanation.surface: A saint and a missionary venture into a remote polar region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saint and missionary' look like a pair of people; the saint is wordplay and the missionary alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An apostle is someone sent to spread a faith, as Paul was, so an evangelist or preacher abroad.

clue.text: Witty comment succeeded, with person cooperating

indicators.note: with means alongside, so one piece is placed next to another

blocks.note: s is the abbreviation for succeeded, as in family trees
an ally is someone who works with you

explanation.surface: A quip landed well thanks to a helpful partner.
explanation.walkthrough: S for succeeded is a genealogy abbreviation used in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: A sally is a quick, clever remark or retort, a burst of wit in conversation.

clue.text: Attending party in NI, doctor by nature smart

indicators.note: to attend is to be present beside, so one piece is placed next to another
by means next to, so pieces sit side by side

blocks.note: Dr is the abbreviation for doctor
esse is Latin for being, one's essential nature
the Democratic Unionist Party of Northern Ireland

explanation.surface: A doctor with a sharp mind goes to a political party meeting in Northern Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: The DUP is a unionist party in Northern Ireland; esse, being or essence, is a philosopher's word for nature.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone dressed up is wearing their best clothes, so they look well groomed and elegant.
